food.text: The Norton tradition developed along the Alaskan shore of the Bering Strait around 1000 BCE. Its people hunted caribou and smaller land mammals while also fishing for salmon and hunting larger sea mammals, combining land and marine food sources.

Communities of the Arctic Small Tool tradition set up camps along coasts and streams to take advantage of seal and salmon populations. Many researchers believe it was these people who first introduced the bow and arrow to the Arctic.

The Dorset culture, which lasted from about 500 BCE, made oil lamps called qulliq, carved from soapstone and filled with seal oil. These lamps were among the culture's signature artifacts, alongside distinctive triangular stone blades.

During the Choris Stage of the Norton tradition, lasting from about 1600 to 500 BCE, people along the northwest Alaskan coast built sizable oval houses and hunted caribou and sea mammals. They made pottery in a style similar to Siberia's, with settlements reaching as far as the Mackenzie River Delta and Banks Island.

Compared to their Arctic Small Tool tradition predecessors, the Norton people were more oriented toward the sea. They brought new technologies into use, including oil-burning lamps and clay pottery vessels.

Norton communities lived in fairly permanent villages with substantial dwellings. During summer months they used small camps for temporary hunting and fishing, before returning to their main dwelling place at the end of the hunting season.

During the Norton stage, lasting from about 500 BCE to 800 CE, people relied on caribou hunting and fishing while refining their pottery, adding check stamps applied with ivory paddles. New stone lamps and ground slate projectile points also came into use.

art.text: The Dorset people, who lived across the Arctic from 500 BCE until as late as 1500 CE, were highly skilled at carving refined miniature figures and striking masks. These works point to an active shamanistic tradition among Dorset artisans.

The Old Bering Sea culture, centered on the Bering Strait region from as early as 200 BCE, developed an elaborate art style built around circle and dot motifs. Nearly every known Old Bering Sea site lies within a kilometer of the ocean, reflecting its deeply maritime life.

At the Ipiutak site on Point Hope, Alaska, a culture that arose as early as 100 to 200 BCE produced elaborately carved objects of ivory, wood, bone, and stone. Excavations there uncovered more than 500 house depressions and over 100 burials filled with striking artwork.

Communities of the Choris Stage, an early phase of Alaska's Norton tradition, lived at coastal sites in northwest Alaska and made fiber-tempered pottery decorated with linear stamped patterns similar to Siberian styles. They also built sizable oval houses while hunting caribou and sea mammals.

Dorset artisans of this same period also crafted qulliq, oil lamps carved from soapstone, alongside distinctive triangular end-blades and small carving tools called burins. These artifacts remain among the clearest evidence of Dorset craftsmanship across the Arctic.

Ipiutak carvers produced ivory objects in a distinctive openwork style, most often depicting animals such as walruses, bears, wolves, birds, loons, and seals. Human figures were comparatively rare. Almost all of these carvings were recovered from shallow burials at the site, where the dead may not have been buried in dug graves at all: their bodies were placed in wooden frames and left at the surface.

In the Norton Stage that followed, pottery became more refined, combining earlier Choris-style stamps with new check stamps applied using ivory paddles. This period also introduced stone oil lamps into Alaska's Norton tradition.

The earliest and sparest Old Bering Sea designs are known as Okvik, named for mounds on an island off the east coast of St. Lawrence Island excavated by Otto Geist. A small Okvik site, the Hillside locality, contains five stone slab houses dated to between 200 and 400 CE.

Dorset culture artifacts include distinctive triangular end-blades, burins and oil lamps called qulliq made of soapstone. The culture lasted in the North American Arctic from 500 BCE to between 1000 and 1500 CE. It is named after Cape Dorset in Nunavut, Canada.

Ipiutak carvers used iron burins, a specialized engraving tool, to create their openwork ivory art. This technical skill helped make the culture, which arose as early as 100 to 200 BCE, especially noted for the elaborateness of its artwork.

The Ipiutak Stage, the final and most artistically developed phase of the Norton tradition, is known for elegant, ornately adorned harpoon heads. Its art consisted mainly of ivory carvings depicting animal and human figures.

The earliest known Old Bering Sea artworks, dated to around 200 BCE, come from mortuary remains at the Ekven cemetery in Chukotka. This makes Ekven a key site for tracing the origins of the culture's circle and dot art style.

science.text: In 325 BC the Greek sailor Pytheas set out to find the source of the tin that reached the Greek colony of Massilia. After sailing past the Pillars of Hercules, he reached Brittany and Cornwall and circled the British Isles. Some scholars believe this was among the first attempts to penetrate the Arctic Circle.

Starting with Aristotle, the Earth was divided into five zones. Two frigid climes, the Arctic and Antarctic, lay around the poles, an uninhabitable torrid clime lay near the equator, and two temperate climes lay between them. This Greek scheme shaped how the polar regions were imagined.

Pytheas reported a land called Thule, where after six days of sailing he reached the edge of a frozen sea that he described as "curdled". He also described what is believed to be the aurora and the midnight sun. Later Greek and Roman authorities such as Strabo regarded his tales as fantasy.

The first century BC Greek astronomer Geminus of Rhodes claimed that the name Thule went back to an archaic word for the polar night phenomenon, "the place where the sun goes to rest". Avienius later added that in summer on Thule night lasted only two hours. This is a clear reference to the midnight sun.

A genetic study published in Science in August 2014 examined the remains of nineteen Dorset people buried in Canada and Greenland between c. 170 BCE and 1320 CE. Their mitochondrial DNA suggested genetic continuity with the earlier Saqqaq culture. The study also found no evidence of genetic mixing between Dorset people and the Greenlandic Norse.

Dorset artifacts include distinctive triangular end-blades, oil lamps called qulliq made of soapstone, and burins. The culture has been defined as having four phases because of distinct differences in hunting and tool-making technologies. The Dorset lasted from 500 BCE.

Pytheas of Massilia described a land he called "Eschate Thule", where the Sun set for only three hours each day. The water there was replaced by a congealed substance "on which one can neither walk nor sail". Today this is thought to describe loose sea ice known as "growlers" or "bergy bits".

Claudius Ptolemy was the first ancient scientist known to devise the system of seven climes. His list of parallels ran north from the equator so that the longest day grew by quarter-hour steps from 12 hours to 18 hours at 58° N. It then reached 24 hours at the Arctic Circle.

The fourth-century commentator Servius wrote that on Thule, when the sun is in Cancer, there are said to be perpetual days without nights. He placed Thule near Orkney and Ireland. Such reports show how ancient writers tried to explain the sun's behavior in the far north.

culture.text: The Dorset were a Paleo-Eskimo culture that lasted from 500 BCE to between 1000 CE and 1500 CE in the North American Arctic. They are named after Cape Dorset, now Kinngait, in Nunavut, Canada. Their artifacts include triangular end-blades, soapstone oil lamps called qulliq, and burins.

Inuit legends tell of the Tuniit, whom they describe as powerful giants living in stone houses. They were believed capable of enormous feats of strength, such as carrying walruses or moving enormous boulders. The Dorset people are probably identical to the Tuniit.

The Dorset were highly skilled at making refined miniature carvings and striking masks. Both are taken to indicate an active shamanistic tradition. Their culture was remarkably homogeneous across the Canadian Arctic, with some variations noted in Greenland and Newfoundland and Labrador.

In 325 BC the Greek sailor Pytheas sailed in search of the source of tin reaching the colony of Massilia. From local people he heard of the mysterious land of Thule to the north. After six days of sailing he reached the edge of a frozen sea, which he described as curdled, and he described what is believed to be the aurora and the midnight sun.

Later Greek and Roman authorities, such as the geographer Strabo, regarded the tales of Pytheas as fantasy. Historians disagree about where his Thule lay. Some claim it was either the Norwegian coast or the Shetland Islands, based on his descriptions and the trade routes of early British sailors.

Dorset history is divided into Dorset I, from 500 BCE to 500 CE, and Dorset II, the following 500 years to 1000 CE. Archaeological evidence shows that between 500 BCE and 500 CE, remarkable technological and cultural advances took place in the Dorset region of northern Canada and Greenland. This period is known as Dorset I.

The Chertov Ovrag site on Wrangel Island, in the Russian Arctic, is the westernmost site of Paleo-Eskimo habitation. Found in 1975, it yielded stone and ivory tools, including a toggle harpoon used for hunting sea mammals. Hunting sea mammals was a significant innovation for Arctic culture, believed to have started from 2000 to 1 BCE.

Independence II culture appeared in northern Greenland from the 8th century BC. It followed Independence I and had a similar geographical extent, though Independence I had occupied northern Greenland much more extensively. Independence I was named after Independence Fjord in Peary Land.

The extreme north of Greenland shaped daily life for the early peoples there. In the High Arctic the sun stays above the horizon for around two to four months each year. The coldest months are lit only by twilight, the aurora, and the circling moon.

A 2014 genetic study examined nineteen Dorset people buried in Canada and Greenland between c. 170 BCE and 1320 CE. It found no evidence of genetic mixing between the Dorset and the Greenlandic Norse. The Dorset were also genetically distinct from the Thule people, who completely replaced them around 1300 CE.
